kg-0073.p.budget.comfort: ≈$300–500/person: CBT/Eurasia tour (from $500 for 2 days at Eurasia) or a car with a driver + Ak-Sai camp $65–85 + a horse $15/hour
kg-0073.p.permits: A border-zone permit is mandatory (border zone of the At-Bashy District near the Chinese border). Ways to get it: 1) tour.too.kg — 3,000 som (all border zones) / $35 for the Kel-Suu–Kok-Kiya–Chatyr-Kul zone; 5–7 working days; office at 105/3 Isanov St., Bishkek (2026). 2) CBT Naryn — €30 (Naryn Region only, ~1 week), €35 (several regions), €50 urgent in 2 working days (stage 1); Nomad's Land: from Naryn it is fastest — in a few days, via Bishkek — up to 2 weeks. Step by step: (1) send a scan of your passport and the trip dates (WhatsApp/form); (2) pay a 50% prepayment; (3) the Border Service reviews it for ~1 week; (4) pick up the paper original in Bishkek or Naryn (or via the guide/tour — then a copy of the passport is sent a few days earlier). The permit is valid for up to 1 month. It is checked at the military posts on the Kyndy pass/at the entrance to the Ak-Sai valley (2 posts per Eurasia Travel) — you need the original permit with a stamp and your passport. Photographing the posts is forbidden. No fee for entering the lake area/valley was found. Chatyr-Kul is part of the Karatal-Japyryk nature reserve (Ramsar): no separate tourist fee was found; approaching the water and disturbing the birds are not allowed.
kg-0073.p.access: The trek is only for the fit (4,000 m); with children and older people, the view of the lake can be had from a car on the Torugart highway (with a permit). A stroller — only from the car. A dog on the trek — not advisable (nature reserve, shepherd dogs).

kg-0077.name: Eki-Naryn Valley
kg-0077.near: The village of Eki-Naryn (in the valley, at the confluence of the rivers); the town of Naryn is about 44 km to the west (open.kg, Journal of Nomads), ~1 h by taxi (TripAdvisor).
kg-0077.elev: About 2250 m (open.kg); the earlier “over 2000 m” does not contradict this.
kg-0077.short: Eki-Naryn (“two Naryns”) is a wooded valley 44 km east of the town of Naryn, at the confluence of the Big and Small Naryn, with spruce-covered slopes, a yurt camp and trails for walks and horse rides.
kg-0077.desc: The name translates from Kyrgyz as “two Naryns”: this is where the Big and Small Naryn merge to form the Naryn River. The valley, at an elevation of about 2250 m, is covered with coniferous (spruce) forest, surrounded by mountains and alpine jailoo (summer pasture); nearby is the Salkyn-Tor National Park, which protects ibexes, deer, wild boar, bears and the snow leopard (open.kg). In summer locals set up yurts here, graze livestock and make felt; archaeologists have found traces of ancient settlements. Foreigners come here relatively rarely — TripAdvisor calls the valley a quiet and wild corner (4.1/5). A gravel road with switchbacks leads from Naryn; further up the Small Naryn runs a canyon through which you can get to Kochkor — that stretch is a dirt road and dangerous in the dark (mykgstan, 2016).
kg-0077.guide: Eki-Naryn is the best short trip out of Naryn into nature: an hour by taxi and you are in a spruce gorge at the place where the Big and Small Naryn meet. The trails start from the bridge — walk along the river and climb the slope to see the confluence from above. Overnight at Akyl's yurt camp: you can take part in cooking and felt-making workshops here, and the host's sons lead hikes and horse rides. Be careful near the cliffs — there are no railings. If you are driving your own car toward Kochkor through the Small Naryn canyon, go through it only in daylight.
kg-0077.see: The confluence of the Big and Small Naryn; spruce slopes and the river valley; trails from the bridge; summer yurts and pastures; Salkyn-Tor National Park nearby; the Small Naryn canyon upstream.
kg-0077.skip: You have only one day in Naryn and are heading on to Tash-Rabat or Kel-Suu — those places are more striking. You want comfort: conditions at the camp are simple. You are traveling with small children — there are no railings at the cliffs.
kg-0077.diff: Easy: walks around the valley and on the trails from the bridge; horse rides and guided hikes — depending on your level. Be careful near unprotected cliffs.
kg-0077.when: June — September (summer yurts, workshops during the summer school holidays — CBT Kyrgyzstan); in autumn — yellow deciduous trees in the valley (not confirmed). The canyon toward Kochkor is dangerous in bad weather.
kg-0077.hours: An open natural area, with no restrictions or permits. Akyl's yurt camp is seasonal (summer), booking via CBT Kyrgyzstan.
kg-0077.daytime: Morning and evening — soft light on the spruce forests and the river confluence; drive the road through the Small Naryn canyon only in daylight (mykgstan).
kg-0077.how: From Naryn by taxi/car about 1 h (≈44 km) on a gravel road with switchbacks (TripAdvisor, open.kg); shared taxis/marshrutkas (minibuses) from Naryn (Journal of Nomads). Alternative — from Kochkor through the Small Naryn canyon (dirt road, daylight only).
kg-0077.needcar: Yes: a taxi or your own car from Naryn; you can try a shared taxi/marshrutka (minibus) to the village of Eki-Naryn.
kg-0077.self: Yes: no permit needed; get there by taxi or your own car, and walk the trails on your own.

kg-0077.stay: Akyl's Yurt Camp Eki Naryn (CBT Kyrgyzstan): 10 yurts for up to 50 guests, two dining yurts, toilets and a shower, cooking and felt workshops, guides; +996 770 443 331, cbtkgreservation@gmail.com. Prices are not given in the sources. Also guesthouses in Naryn (CBT Naryn).

kg-0077.entry: Free: an open natural area, no permits or fees found (entry to Salkyn-Tor National Park is a separate site, its fee was not checked).

kg-0077.bring: Comfortable shoes for the trails, a windbreaker and a warm layer (≈2250 m), tick and insect repellent for the forest (recommendation), water and a snack, cash for the camp.
kg-0077.warn: There are no railings at the cliffs — watch children (TripAdvisor). The Small Naryn canyon is a dangerous dirt road, do not drive it in the dark (mykgstan). The rivers are fast and cold — do not wade across without experience.
kg-0077.food: At Akyl's camp — home-style Kyrgyz cooking and cooking workshops (CBT Kyrgyzstan): beshbarmak, boorsok, kaymak (editorial).
kg-0077.reviews: TripAdvisor: 4.1/5, 10 reviews, No. 5 of 16 in Naryn (as of 07.10.2026). Google Maps — no unambiguous listing (checked 03.10.2026). Pros — beautiful wild views, quiet, easy trails, horse rides; cons — no railings at the cliffs, remoteness, one negative review about the reception at the yurt camp.

kg-0077.p.sum: Eki-Naryn is a wooded valley at the confluence of the Big and Small Naryn, ≈44 km from Naryn (≈1 h by taxi on gravel with switchbacks); no permit needed. Get to Naryn by the Bishkek — Naryn marshrutka (minibus) (600 som) or by plane (2100 som), then take a shared taxi/marshrutka (minibus) from Naryn or a taxi via CBT Naryn. The base is Akyl's yurt camp (Akyl's Yurt Camp, CBT: +996 770 443 331) with horses and guides; on the way is Salkyn-Tor National Park (entry 20 som). The Small Naryn canyon toward Kochkor is for 4×4 only and in daylight only.

kg-0078.name: Lake Kel-Suu
kg-0078.near: There are no permanent villages nearby: the base is the yurt camps in the Kok-Kyya valley (≈20 yurts, end of the road; about 8–12 km on foot to the lake). The last sizeable settlement is At-Bashy; the city of Naryn is 150–200 km by road (sources disagree). The earlier “Karaul-Tobe ~38.5 km” is a straight-line distance across the mountain ridges and is no guide for the trip.
kg-0078.elev: About 3500 m (too.kg, Kabar, kgnomad); TripAdvisor says 3520 m, the Trip to Kyrgyzstan catalogue 3514 m. Water level and surface area change noticeably from season to season and year to year.
kg-0078.short: Kel-Suu is a narrow turquoise lake at ~3500 m in a rocky canyon near the Chinese border (At-Bashy District), with a vanishing water level and boat rides between sheer walls.
kg-0078.desc: The lake lies in a narrow canyon between sheer cliffs in the southeast of Naryn Region, about 20 km from the Chinese border, and feeds the Kok-Kyya River. Its length varies by source from 9 km (too.kg) to ~12 km of canyon (Kabar) and 17 km (TripAdvisor); the width ranges from a few dozen metres to 2 km. Kabar links the lake's formation to a landslide in the 1980s, while kg24.news calls it a glacial water body in a fissure; what they agree on is that the water periodically drains into underground grottoes and the level changes dramatically (the last big drop was in 2018), hence the Kyrgyz “kel-suu” — “coming water”. In summer the water is 8–10 °C, and the weather changes within minutes: sun, rain, wind, hail. Access is only with a border permit, through the checkpoint after the Kyndy Pass and the yurt camps in the Kok-Kyya valley. With the growth in tourist numbers in 2026, litter has become a problem (time.kg, 14.08.2026), and the Ministry of Transport checked boatmen for registration and documents (24.08.2026).
kg-0078.guide: The main thing at Kel-Suu is a motorboat ride deep into the canyon: the walls rise straight out of the turquoise water, and only from the water do you see how long the lake really is. Head to the lake in the morning — the fords on the Kok-Kyya rise by 30–50 cm after lunch, and dozens of people gather at the shore by midday. Look at the dark caves in the cliffs: according to local stories, the lake's water drains into underground grottoes from time to time, which is why it looks different every year. Don't be surprised if you find it lower than in photos — that's normal. Take your litter with you: in 2026 the shores became noticeably dirtier, and locals are talking about it.
kg-0078.see: A canyon with sheer walls and turquoise water — best seen from a motorboat (30 min — about 1000 som/person, 2024–2025); caves and grottoes in the cliffs; the ford and the Kok-Kyya river valley with yaks; the ~8–12 km footpath (2–3 h one way) from the camps to the lake; the road via Ak-Say and the Kyndy Pass (3400 m).
kg-0078.skip: You have fewer than 3 full days from Bishkek (5 from Almaty) — the road will take almost all your time. You can't get the border permit in time (from a few working days to 2 weeks). You don't tolerate an altitude of ~3500 m and cold nights down to −5 °C in a yurt without amenities.
kg-0078.diff: Moderate: the road is difficult (4×4 jeep, fords), while the walk itself is ~12 km round trip with almost no elevation gain (OunTravela) with a river ford; alternatively, ride a horse or take a UAZ “bukhanka”/GAZ-66 for the last ~8 km. The main difficulties are the 3500 m altitude, the weather and the river level.
kg-0078.when: Mid-July to late August (NomadCar); the yurt camps operate from about late June to early September (kgnomad; too.kg — mid-June to early September). Snow is possible in June, nights are frosty in September, and the road is impassable in winter. The lake level is higher in July–September (TripAdvisor).
kg-0078.hours: An open natural area, but only with a border permit; the camps operate seasonally (late June — early September). The permit is checked at the post after the Kyndy Pass.
kg-0078.daytime: Morning: there is less water in the Kok-Kyya River (after lunch the level rises by 30–50 cm — NomadCar), fewer people at the lake (TripAdvisor), and calmer water for the boat. Leave the camp at dawn.
kg-0078.how: Bishkek → Naryn (≈350 km of paved road) → At-Bashy → Kyndy Pass (3400 m) and the border post → Ak-Say valley → Kok-Kyya valley (end of the road, yurt camps). From there it is 8–12 km to the lake on foot, on horseback or by UAZ/GAZ-66. From Naryn to the camps it is 150–200 km over gravel and fords, 4–8 h (Kabar: 150–160 km, 5–6 h; OunTravela: ~200 km, 4–5 h; NomadCar: 120 km of gravel + 60–80 km of fords). The total journey from Bishkek is 10–12 h.
kg-0078.needcar: Yes: a 4×4 SUV is a must (ground clearance of 200–220 mm or more, low-range gear) with a local driver, or a tour; there is no public transport.
kg-0078.self: Partly: you can arrange the permit yourself through CBT Naryn or tour.too.kg, but driving without an experienced local driver and a prepared 4×4 is not recommended (fords, no signal, difficult navigation — Freedom Travel 2025). The walk from the camps can be done on your own (sea2peak, no guide).
kg-0078.roadtype: Paved up to Naryn; Naryn — At-Bashy — Kyndy — Ak-Say is gravel/washboard (≈120 km); the last 60–80 km have boggy stretches and fords (NomadCar). In August 2026 road maintenance unit no. 20 of At-Bashy District graded the At-Bashy — Kyndy — Torugart road (time.kg). The last 8–12 km to the lake are a trail and a ford.
kg-0078.traveltime: Bishkek — Naryn ~5–6 h; Naryn — Kok-Kyya camps 4–8 h (OunTravela 4–5 h; Kabar 5–6 h; kgnomad 5–8 h); camp — lake 2–3 h on foot one way. From Almaty to Ak-Say — 15–16 h (Freedom Travel, 07.2025). At least 3 days from Bishkek.
kg-0078.stay: Yurt camps in the Kok-Kyya valley: Kel-Suu Yurt Camp (2GIS: from 1800 som, up to 40 beds, breakfast, cafe, horse rides, Wi-Fi; +996 552 979 696; rating 4.7/30), Golden Moon (often mentioned — kgnomad), Jyrgal's Yurt Camp (video). 2024 prices (too.kg): a yurt for 2 with breakfast — 1700 som/person, a yurt for 4–7 — 1500 som/person, a “hotel” room with breakfast — 2000 som/person, meals — 800 som per meal; kgnomad (2026): 1500–2500+ som/person with meals. Tent camping is possible (sea2peak).
kg-0078.net: There is practically no mobile signal after leaving Naryn/the last villages (NomadCar, too.kg, kgnomad 2026); a weak signal sometimes on the passes. Some camps have Wi-Fi (Kel-Suu Yurt Camp per 2GIS; Kabar) — probably satellite, quality not confirmed.
kg-0078.entry: No separate entrance fee for the lake was found. A border permit is mandatory: CBT Naryn — €30 (Naryn Region only, 1 week), €35 (several regions), €50 rush in 2 working days; tour.too.kg — 3000 som (all border zones, 7 working days, 2026); too.kg (2024) — 2600 som for a foreigner, 3–4 working days.
kg-0078.transfer: Jeep Naryn — Kok-Kyya — Naryn with waiting: 13,000–20,000+ som per car (≈3500–5000 som/person with 4 passengers, kgnomad 07.2026). UAZ/GAZ-66 to the lake: 10,000 som per group round trip (too.kg 2024). Marshrutka (minibus) Bishkek — Naryn — 600 som (CBT Naryn, 05.2026). A 3-day group tour from Bishkek — from 14,900 ₽ (tour.too.kg, 2026).
kg-0078.bring: Your border permit (original/printout) and passport; a warm jacket and hat (down to −5 °C at night, hail by day), a rain jacket; sunscreen and sunglasses — sunburn is common (Freedom Travel); shoes for the ford or sandals; cash in som (no ATMs); a flashlight, a power bank; a bag for litter; a first-aid kit including altitude-sickness remedies.
kg-0078.warn: Border zone next to the Chinese border: without a permit you will be turned back at the post after the Kyndy Pass. The Kok-Kyya River rises 30–50 cm after lunch, and the ford is impassable during floods (NomadCar, Freedom Travel) — cross in the morning. Altitude ~3500 m, abrupt weather changes, water 8–10 °C. Only get into boats with life jackets: in 08.2026 some boatmen turned out to have no documents (time.kg). There is no signal. The lake level can be low — photos online don't guarantee the view.
kg-0078.food: The yurt camps serve simple home cooking: beshbarmak, shorpo, boorsok, kaimak, tea, sometimes kumis (meals ~800 som each — too.kg 2024). On the way — lagman at a cafe in Naryn (Freedom Travel, 2025).
kg-0078.reviews: TripAdvisor: 4.9/5, 43 reviews, no. 1 of 15 in Naryn (as of 07.10.2026). Google Maps: 4.8/5, 99 ratings (as of 03.10.2026, catalogue cross-check). 2GIS — Kel-Suu Yurt Camp: 4.7/5, 30 ratings. Pros — “the most beautiful place”, turquoise water, a boat ride through the canyon, the road via Ak-Say. Cons — a long, hard road, low water levels in some seasons, crowds in peak season, litter (2026).
kg-0078.p.sum: Kel-Suu is in the border zone by China: first arrange a permit (tour.too.kg 3000 som/$35 or CBT Naryn €30–50, 5–7 working days), then allow 2–3 days: Naryn → At-Bashy → Kyndy Pass (2 border posts) → Ak-Say → the Kok-Kyya yurt camps (≈145–160 km, 4.5–6 h by 4×4). You spend the night in a yurt (1500–2500 som with meals), and in the morning go 7.5–9 km on foot, on horseback (≈2000–2500 som) or by UAZ (10,000 som/car) to the lake and take a boat ride through the canyon (≈1000 som/30 min). The easiest option is a group tour with tour.too.kg ($195 from Bishkek) or a 2-day tour from Naryn; on your own — only with a local driver and a full tank from Naryn.

kg-0078.p.iti.0.title: 2 days from Naryn
kg-0078.p.iti.0.plan: Day 1: 9:00 departure from Globus (Naryn) → At-Bashy → Kyndy (posts) → Ak-Say → lunch/evening in a Kok-Kyya yurt (≈5 h on the road). Day 2: 7:00 breakfast, in the morning (while the water is low) 2–3 h to the lake on foot/horseback/UAZ, a 30-min boat ride, a picnic; 13:00 back to camp, 14:00 departure, ≈19:00 Naryn.
kg-0078.p.iti.1.title: 3 days from Bishkek
kg-0078.p.iti.1.plan: Day 1: 08:00 Bishkek → Boom Gorge → Orto-Tokoy → lunch in Naryn → evening at the Kok-Kyya camp (≈460 km). Day 2: the lake (hike/horse/boat). Day 3: back via Bozogo, lunch in Naryn, evening in Bishkek (tour.too.kg itinerary).
kg-0078.p.iti.2.title: A logical combination
kg-0078.p.iti.2.plan: Kel-Suu + Kok-Kyya valley + Ak-Say (one road) → on the way back Koshoy-Korgon (near Kara-Suu) → Tash-Rabat and Chatyr-Kol (with the same permit) → Naryn → Song-Kol via Dolon/Kalmak-Ashuu. 6–8 days as a loop (like the Journal of Nomads overland tour “Kel Suu, Tash Rabat and Son Kul”).
kg-0078.p.iti.3.title: From the west via Chatyr-Kol
kg-0078.p.iti.3.plan: Tash-Rabat → the Bishkek—Kashgar highway → along Chatyr-Kol → Ak-Say valley → Kok-Kyya: 205 km in a day (Nomad's Land) — with one permit it combines Tash-Rabat, Chatyr-Kol and Kel-Suu without returning to Naryn.
kg-0078.p.season: June: snow is possible, the camps open toward the end of June, high water at the fords. July — August: the best time, the lake is full, the camps are open, +15…+20 by day, around 0 °C at night, hail. September: camps until ≈25.09, night frosts, few people, lower water. October — May: the Ak-Say road is under snow (down to −40…−56 °C), since 2025 there has been a winter festival in February, in winter only organized groups. Few mosquitoes, but horseflies near the herds.
kg-0078.p.budget.economy: ≈14,000–18,000 som/person for 3 days in a group of 4: marshrutka Bishkek—Naryn 600×2; jeep Naryn—Kok-Kyya—Naryn 13,000–20,000 som/4 ≈3500–5000; permit 3000; yurt 2 nights with breakfast and dinner ≈3000–4200 (1500–2100/night, JoN 2026); horse 2000–2500 or walking 0; boat 1000; a night in Naryn ~1500–2500.
kg-0078.p.budget.comfort: ≈$195–350 for a tour (tour.too.kg group tour $195 from Bishkek or JoN €230–350 from Naryn) + horse ~$20 + boat ~$15 + lunches ~$10 = ≈20,000–35,000 som/person.
kg-0078.p.permits: A border permit is mandatory (border zone of At-Bashy District by the Chinese border). Ways to get it: 1) tour.too.kg — 3000 som (all border zones) / $35 for the Kel-Suu—Kok-Kyya—Chatyr-Kol zone; 5–7 working days; office at 105/3 Isanov St., Bishkek (2026). 2) CBT Naryn — €30 (Naryn Region only, ~1 week), €35 (several regions), €50 rush in 2 working days (stage 1); Nomad's Land: from Naryn it is quickest — within a few days, via Bishkek — up to 2 weeks. Step by step: (1) send a scan of your passport and your travel dates (WhatsApp/form); (2) pay a 50% prepayment; (3) the Border Service reviews it for ~1 week; (4) pick up the paper original in Bishkek or Naryn (or via a guide/tour — in which case a copy of your passport is sent several days ahead). The permit is valid for up to 1 month. It is checked at the military posts at the Kyndy Pass/at the entrance to the Ak-Say valley (2 posts per Eurasia Travel) — you need the original permit with a stamp, and your passport. Photographing the posts is prohibited. No entrance fee for the lake/valley was found. JoN (04.2026) advises applying for the permit through CBT Naryn at least 2 weeks ahead; if you travel on your own, your driver needs a permit too.
kg-0078.p.access: With children — only school-age and if they tolerate altitude well (3500 m, 5–6 h of bumpy road, fords); Tripster writes “not suitable for children”. For older people — hard because of the road and altitude; you can reach the lake by UAZ. With a stroller — not accessible. With a dog — technically possible in your own car, but not recommended in the border zone and among shepherd dogs.

kg-0079.name: Kok-Moynok Canyons
kg-0079.dist: Territory of the town of Balykchy
kg-0079.near: Kok-Moynok-2 village (Kok-Moynok Ekinchi) — the access road goes through it; Balykchy — 11–12.5 km.
kg-0079.elev: 1,500–1,700 m above sea level (Asiamixtravel); elevation gain from the parking lot to the upper points — up to 170 m (hiking.kg).
kg-0079.short: Kok-Moynok is a labyrinth of red-and-yellow sandstone canyons and “towers” above the Chu River at the exit of the Boom Gorge, 165 km from Bishkek and 12 km from Balykchy.
kg-0079.desc: The Kok-Moynok Canyons (“green hollow/blue isthmus”) lie on the right bank of the Chu between the Boom Gorge and the Orto-Tokoy Reservoir, beyond the village of Kok-Moynok-2. It is a network of dry erosion gullies up to 200 m deep in red and yellow sandstones and clays: narrow corridors, the “Rocket” rock in the middle of the main canyon, and viewpoint hills overlooking the Chu. The place can be seen in 2–3 hours: from the parking lot to the main formations it is about 1.3 km and up to 170 m of gain. In dry weather a passenger car can reach it, but after rain the dirt road along the river turns to mud and the dry channels may fill with water. There is no infrastructure; locals charge a token fee for driving in (50–300 som according to reviews), and in the off-season it is sometimes free.
kg-0079.guide: Turn off the highway at the fuel station before Balykchy towards Kochkor, cross the bridge over the Chu and follow the dirt road along the river through Kok-Moynok-2 — another 5–7 km and the parking lot is in front of you. From there it is 20–30 minutes up the wide channel to a “city” of towers: find the “Rocket” rock and climb any hill — from there you can see the turquoise Chu and the layered walls. Go through the narrow corridors with a partner, not alone, and only if no rain is expected: a downpour turns these channels into a torrent within minutes. The best light is in the evening, when the sun hits the red walls from the side; in summer by day it is scorching with no shade. This is not Konorchek: to reach it you have to walk 5 km from the highway, whereas here you can drive almost right up — which is why Kok-Moynok makes a handy stop on the way to Issyk-Kul or Song-Kol.
kg-0079.see: Narrow erosion passages, sandstone towers and viewpoint hills; the “Rocket” rock; a panorama of the Chu River and the Boom Gorge; wild horses on the approaches; sunset light on the red walls.
kg-0079.skip: You're already going to Konorchek or Skazka (Fairy Tale) — the geology is similar, and Kok-Moynok is smaller. It's raining or rain is expected — the channels are dangerous and the dirt road turns to mud. A summer midday with children — hot and no shade.
kg-0079.diff: Easy: 2/5 on foot on the hiking.kg scale, up to 1.3 km from the parking lot and up to 170 m of gain; the drive in is 3/5 because of the dirt road. Suitable for families with children; be careful in the narrow corridors — the rock crumbles.
kg-0079.when: May–October (Asiamixtravel); spring and autumn are more comfortable than summer (hot by day). In winter it is usually accessible — there is little snow. Don't go in the rain or right after it.
kg-0079.hours: Open area, open 24 hours; no ticket offices, though locals may charge a fee on the approach (see “Entry cost”).
kg-0079.daytime: The second half of the day and sunset (the “golden hour”) — side light on the red walls, with no backlight when walking up the channel; sunrise is also good but colder.
kg-0079.how: From Bishkek along the A-365 highway through the Boom Gorge ~165 km (2.5–3 h); before Balykchy, turn onto the Kochkor/Naryn road, turn off at the Bishkek Petroleum fuel station, cross the bridge over the Chu and then follow 4–7 km of dirt road along the river through the village of Kok-Moynok-2 to the parking lot at the canyon (5 minutes after the village there is a fork — go left). From Balykchy 12.5 km (25–35 min), from Kochkor ~45 km (~1 h). Public transport does not run to the canyon.
kg-0079.needcar: Yes: 4–7 km of dirt road from the highway; you can walk from the highway, but it is long and dusty. A passenger car can make it in dry weather.
kg-0079.self: Yes: the route from the parking lot along the channel is obvious, no permits are needed; take an offline map (Maps.me/2GIS), water and closed shoes; don't go into the narrow side branches alone.
kg-0079.roadtype: Paved road along the A-365 to the turn-off; then a dirt road along the Chu through Kok-Moynok-2 (4–7 km), in places right at the water; in dry weather passable by a passenger car with care (low ground clearance — be careful), after rain only high clearance/4x4. In the canyon — sand and rocks, unmarked trails.
kg-0079.traveltime: Bishkek — parking lot 2 h 45 min — 3 h (165 km); Balykchy — 25–35 min; Kochkor — ~1 h. The walking part is up to 1.3 km and up to 1.5 h one way; 2–3 h for the whole visit.
kg-0079.stay: There is no accommodation on site (camping is possible, but there is no infrastructure). The nearest: hotels and guesthouses in Balykchy (12 km), CBT and guesthouses in Kochkor (45 km), guest houses on the west shore of Issyk-Kul. A landmark on the highway is the roadside café Ak-Jol. 2025–2026 prices are not confirmed.
kg-0079.net: There is coverage in the villages of Kok-Moynok and by the highway; inside the canyons the signal drops out behind the walls (a general pattern in the Boom Gorge; there are no reports by operator). Download offline maps.
kg-0079.entry: There is no official fee. According to 2GIS reviews (2024–2026), locals on the approach/parking lot charge 50–300 som per person; an April 2024 blog says free; hiking.kg warns of a possible fee at the main parking lot without giving an amount. Ask what the fee is for.
kg-0079.transfer: Taxi from Bishkek with waiting ~6,000 som/car (July 2024); Asiamixtravel jeep tour $324 per group of up to 4 people with breakfast (2025); Bishkek — Balykchy train 40–60 som (summer 2024).
kg-0079.bring: Water (1–1.5 L/person), a hat and sun protection (no shade), closed shoes with a non-slip sole, a charged phone with offline maps, a windbreaker, a snack, wet wipes; cash in small notes for a possible fee.
kg-0079.warn: Heavy rain quickly fills the dry channels with water — in a downpour turn back immediately; don't enter the narrow gullies alone. The rocks crumble — don't climb the walls. In summer it is extremely hot by day; in 2024 tours were cancelled because of the heat. After rain the dirt road by the river turns to mud. An unofficial fee on the approach is possible (50–300 som). Respect the wild horses — don't approach them.
kg-0079.food: On the highway near Balykchy — roadside cafés (lagman, manty, shashlik; landmark Ak-Jol); in Balykchy — Issyk-Kul fish (smoked, fried), lunch ~1,500 som/person in local cafés according to a tour operator (2025). There is no food in the canyon.
kg-0079.reviews: 2GIS “Kok-Moynok Canyons”: 4.9/5, 255 ratings, 39 reviews (viewed 07.10.2026). Google Maps: the listing could not be matched (meta: ambiguous result). Pros: impressive red rocks “like in the USA”, deserted, accessible in an ordinary car, a beautiful sunset; cons: summer heat, no toilets or water, crumbling rocks, mud after rain, inconsistent fees for driving in (50–300 som).
kg-0079.p.sum: Kok-Moynok is the most accessible “red” canyon on the road from Bishkek to Issyk-Kul or Song-Kol (≈165 km, 2.5–3 h). Before Balykchy turn towards Kochkor at the fuel station, cross the bridge over the Chu and drive 4–7 km of dirt road through Kok-Moynok-2 to the parking lot. Then 1.3 km and up to 170 m of gain along the channel to the “Rocket” and the viewpoint hills, 2–3 h for everything. In dry weather a passenger car can make it too. Without a car — a day tour from Bishkek (too.kg from $195 per car, 2026) or a marshrutka (minibus)/train to Balykchy and a taxi. Locals sometimes charge 50–300 som on the approach: have small notes.

kg-0080.name: Suusamyr Valley
kg-0080.near: Kaysar — ~4.9 km in a straight line from the catalogue point (OSM); the valley also has the villages of Suusamyr and Kojomkul (the Kojomkul mazar (shrine) and museum — too.kg, eurasia.travel).
kg-0080.elev: Average elevation — about 2,200–2,300 m (eurasia.travel, too.kg); in different parts of the valley — 2,000–3,200 m (Trip to Kyrgyzstan); the surrounding peaks — up to 4,500 m.
kg-0080.short: Suusamyr is a high-mountain valley ~155 km long and up to 40 km wide at ~2,200 m between the Kyrgyz, Talas and Suusamyr ranges: the country's best pastures, yurts, kumys and the Bishkek — Osh highway.
kg-0080.desc: The Suusamyr Valley is an intermontane basin of the Inner Tian Shan in the Jayyl district of the Chuy region, about 160 km southwest of Bishkek. Its length is around 150–155 km, its width up to 40 km, and its average elevation 2,200–2,300 m. The Suusamyr and West Karakol rivers flow through the valley and merge to form the Kokomeren. In summer it is a “green sea” of tall-grass pastures — some of the best in the country: shepherds set up yurts and make kumys and ayran, and kumys-therapy sanatoriums operate; in winter there is deep snow and severe frost, and a ski base operates near the Too-Ashuu Pass. There are more than 300 plant species here and snow leopards live in the area; burial mounds and stone statues (from the 6th century BC) have survived. In the village of Kojomkul there is the mazar (shrine) of the legendary hero Kojomkul with handprints, and a museum. In 1992 the valley was shaken by the strong Suusamyr earthquake (M≈7.3).
kg-0080.guide: Suusamyr is best seen right after the Too-Ashuu tunnel: the valley opens up below as a green carpet to the horizon. In summer stop at the yurts along the highway and try fresh kumys — here it is considered one of the best in the country. If you have a day, turn off to the village of Kojomkul to see the hero's mazar with its “handprints” and the local museum. It is cold at night in the valley even in July (2,200 m), so bring warm clothes if you're staying overnight in a yurt camp. In early summer locals pick steppe mushrooms here, and paragliders catch the thermals above the treeless slopes.
kg-0080.see: The panorama of the valley from the descent after the Too-Ashuu tunnel; summer pastures with yurts and herds; the confluence of the Suusamyr and West Karakol (the source of the Kokomeren); the Kojomkul mazar and museum in the village of the same name; burial mounds and stone statues; the Too-Ashuu ski base in winter.
kg-0080.skip: You're not driving the Bishkek — Osh highway or heading to Talas — 2.5 h one way specifically for the valley is only justified with a night in a yurt. You expect “sights” — the main thing here is open space and pastures. You're travelling in late autumn/winter without winter tyres.
kg-0080.diff: Easy: most of it is accessible from the paved highway, and walks across the pastures involve no elevation gain. Keep in mind the altitude of ~2,200 m (cool, and some people feel slightly short of breath). Side dirt roads to the pastures depend on the weather and sometimes require an SUV.
kg-0080.when: May–July — the “green sea” of pastures (eurasia.travel); June–September — the yurt and kumys season; early summer — mushrooms. In winter (December–March) — snow, severe frost and skiing at Too-Ashuu; the highway is open, but restrictions are possible during snowfall (24.kg, 02.2026).
kg-0080.hours: Open natural area, open 24 hours; the Bishkek — Osh highway runs year-round with temporary restrictions in bad weather. Yurt camps — mostly in summer (Turan Camp is advertised as operating all year).
kg-0080.daytime: Morning and evening — soft light over the pastures and less wind; in summer thunderstorms are possible by day. It is cold at night even in summer (editorial note, from the ~2,200 m altitude).
kg-0080.how: From Bishkek along the Bishkek — Osh highway through Kara-Balta and the tunnel at the Too-Ashuu Pass (~150–160 km, about 2–2.5 h; rome2rio — 153 km, 2 h 17 min). Marshrutkas (minibuses) and shared taxis towards Suusamyr, Talas, Toktogul and Osh leave from Bishkek's bus stations (too.kg).
kg-0080.needcar: Yes: the valley is 2+ h from Bishkek and very extended — you need a car, a taxi or intercity transport. Getting around within the valley without a car is difficult.
kg-0080.self: Yes: by car or by intercity marshrutka/taxi; yurt camps and guesthouses accept guests without a tour. There is mobile coverage in the valley.
kg-0080.roadtype: The paved Bishkek — Osh highway crosses the valley; side roads to the villages are partly paved, and to the pastures dirt (the surface type is not uniform by section).
kg-0080.traveltime: Bishkek → Suusamyr: ~2 h 15 min — 2.5 h by car (rome2rio 153 km; too.kg/eurasia — 160 km). From the Too-Ashuu tunnel to the central part of the valley — 15–20 min.
kg-0080.stay: Turan Camp ethno-camp (Suusamyr village): double yurt 4,000 som, upgraded 6,000 som, four-bed 8,000 som per night with breakfast, kumys, horse rides, archery range (meiman.kg, 2026; +996 550 993 993). Guesthouses, cafés and shops in the valley villages (too.kg); the Too-Ashuu ski base (66 beds + cottages, asiamixtravel); kumys-therapy sanatoriums in summer.
kg-0080.net: Too.kg: there is mobile coverage throughout the valley; on remote pastures and on the pass the coverage may drop out. The operator is not specified.
kg-0080.entry: There is no entrance fee for the valley. What you pay for is passage through the highway tunnels (50 som for a Kyrgyz-registered passenger car / 200 som for a foreign one, since 01.01.2024) and camp services.
kg-0080.transfer: Shared taxi Bishkek — Osh 2,500 som per seat (2026; to Suusamyr it is cheaper — price not confirmed); taxi $19–24 according to rome2rio; tunnel fee 50 som/car. Marshrutka fares to Suusamyr were not found.
kg-0080.bring: Warm clothes even in summer (2,200 m, cold nights), a rain jacket, sun protection (open pastures), cash for kumys and yurts; get water in the villages — drinking river water is not recommended (too.kg). In winter — winter tyres and a reserve of fuel.
kg-0080.warn: In winter — severe frost, snowfall and restrictions on the Too-Ashuu Pass (24.kg 13.02.2026). Don't drink river water (livestock graze there). A seismically active zone (1992 earthquake). On the pastures — shepherds' dogs; don't approach herds without their owners. At an altitude of ~2,200 m it is cool and the sun is harsh.
kg-0080.food: Kumys is the main gastronomic highlight: shepherds make it on the summer jailoo (pastures), and kumys-therapy sanatoriums operate (too.kg, eurasia.travel); ayran; Kyrgyz cuisine in roadside yurts and cafés along the highway; at Turan Camp — breakfast included, lunch and dinner from the menu.
kg-0080.reviews: Google Maps (Susamyr Valley): 4.8/5, 41 ratings (03.10.2026). Traveller reviews (YouTube, blogs): pros — endless pastures, kumys, “the most beautiful road in Kyrgyzstan”; cons — cold at night, simple service, long distances.
kg-0080.p.sum: Suusamyr is a high-mountain jailoo (summer pasture) valley (~2,200 m) 2–2.5 h from Bishkek beyond the Too-Ashuu Pass; the Bishkek — Osh highway runs straight through it. It is most convenient with your own car (tunnel fee 50/200 som) or with a tour. Without a car — a marshrutka or a seat-by-seat taxi towards Osh/Talas/Toktogul, getting off in the valley (to Osh a seat costs 2,500 som, to Suusamyr it is cheaper, but the exact fare was not found). In summer (June–September) yurts selling kumys stand along the highway (a litre nationwide costs 200–350 som, 2026). You can stay overnight at the Turan Camp ethno-camp (yurt 4,000–8,000 som with breakfast, horses, archery), the Altai guesthouse in Suusamyr village or Suus Lodge (double room $40). In winter there are frosts down to −30 and skiing at Too-Ashuu.

kg-0081.name: Dungan Mosque
kg-0081.near: Karakol; the mosque is in the city — 140–142a Abdrakhmanov St., at the corner of Bektenov St. (the central Ibrahim-azhy mosque).
kg-0081.elev: About 1700–1750 m (central Karakol lies at 1690–1770 m; calculated from the city's elevation, there are no point measurements for the mosque).
kg-0081.short: A wooden mosque in the Chinese pagoda style, built by the Dungans in 1907–1910 without a single nail — Karakol's main landmark and a working mosque.
kg-0081.desc: The Dungan Mosque was built by the Dungan community — Chinese Muslims who fled to Semirechye after the uprising of 1877. In 1907 the master Zhou Si arrived from Beijing with a team of ~20 carvers, roofers and masons; three years went into preparing materials, assembly took three months, and the mosque opened on 10 May 1910. The 27×15 m rectangular building of Tian Shan spruce, elm, poplar and walnut is assembled with grooves and tenons, with no nails; it has a multi-tiered roof with upturned corners, carved eaves with dragons, phoenixes and lions, and symbolic colours: red columns (protection from evil), a green roof (well-being), yellow details (wealth). In the 1930s the minaret was torn down and the mosque was closed, but the building survived; the minaret was restored a decade later. Today it is Karakol's working central Ibrahim-azhy mosque and one of the two surviving Dungan mosques in the former USSR.
kg-0081.guide: Walk to the rear of the courtyard — that gives the best angle on the tiered roof with upturned corners, which looks like a Buddhist temple; from the front, the fence and trees block the view. Look closely at the carving under the eaves: dragons, phoenixes and lions — Chinese mythology on a Muslim building, and not a single nail in 115 years. You aren't always let inside: it is a working mosque, and during prayer (especially on Friday 13:00–14:30) viewing is from outside only; women are given a robe and a headscarf at the entrance. Allow 15–20 minutes and combine it with the Holy Trinity Cathedral a kilometre away — two wooden churches of the same era. When you come out, head to the bazaar for ashlan-fu: it is a Dungan dish, and Karakol makes it best in the country.
kg-0081.see: The tiered pagoda roof and carved eaves with dragons and phoenixes; painted columns and beams; assembly without nails; the restored minaret; the courtyard with a garden; the women's section with a separate entrance.
kg-0081.skip: You aren't interested in architecture — viewing from outside takes 10–15 minutes, the grounds are small, and the interior is often closed. You're in Karakol on Friday at midday prayer — access is limited.
kg-0081.diff: Very easy: a city walk, entry from the street, steps at the entrance.
kg-0081.when: Year-round; in summer (June–September) there are more tourists and tours, in winter it's quiet. Avoid Friday prayer (13:00–14:30) and big holidays (Oraza Ait, Kurman Ait), when the mosque is packed.
kg-0081.hours: For tourists daily ~08:00–18:00 (Destination Karakol, undated); 2GIS gives no hours; entry inside depends on services — prayers on Fridays 13:00–14:30. Google Maps: “Daily: 24 hours” (as a working mosque).
kg-0081.daytime: Morning after 9:00 or around 18:00 (evening light on the facade; TripAdvisor reviews advise ~18:00 and hours without groups). Avoid 13:00–14:30 on Friday.
kg-0081.how: Karakol, 140–142a Abdrakhmanov St., at the corner of Bektenov St. — 10–15 minutes on foot from the central square and the bazaar; city marshrutkas (minibuses) (no. 109/111 and others, 20 som in 2024) and taxis (Yandex Go). From Bishkek to Karakol is ~400 km: marshrutkas from the new bus station (1/1 Alma-Atinskaya St.), the GoBus shuttle (450 som in 2022–2023), ~500 som by marshrutka (summer 2024), 6–7 h.
kg-0081.needcar: No — on foot around the city; a taxi is handy if your lodging is on the outskirts.
kg-0081.self: Yes: entry is free with a small fee/donation; follow the dress code (covered arms and legs, a headscarf for women — provided at the entrance), take off your shoes inside, don't photograph people praying.
kg-0081.roadtype: City streets of Karakol (paved) up to the Bektenov/Abdrakhmanov intersection; a pedestrian entrance into the courtyard through the gate.
kg-0081.traveltime: From the centre of Karakol 10–15 min on foot; viewing 10–20 min from outside, up to 30–40 min with a guided tour. Bishkek — Karakol 6–7 h by marshrutka (minibus).
kg-0081.stay: Karakol has dozens of options: guesthouses and hostels (budget ~1000–2000 som/person, 2024–2025 per reports), the “Turkestan” yurt camp in the city (karakol.kg), mid-range hotels; book via Booking/Destination Karakol. Check specific 2026 rates when booking.
kg-0081.net: Full Beeline, O!, MegaCom (4G) coverage in Karakol; Wi-Fi in guesthouses and cafes.
kg-0081.entry: A small fee to enter the grounds: 20–50 som (2GIS: 20–50 som, free for Muslims; a summer 2024 report — 50 som for the garden; Destination Karakol and TripAdvisor 2019 — 20 som). Sometimes a donation is requested. There is no official 2026 rate.
kg-0081.transfer: City marshrutka (minibus) 20 som (2024); Bishkek — Karakol marshrutka ~500 som (2024), GoBus 450 som (2022–2023); a taxi around the city — by the app's meter.
kg-0081.bring: A scarf and clothing that covers arms, legs and head (for women; hooded robes are provided at the entrance), shoes that are easy to take off, small cash (20–50 som), a camera — photos from outside are allowed, inside and of people — with permission.
kg-0081.warn: A working mosque: during prayer (Friday 13:00–14:30 and the five daily prayers) tourists are not admitted inside — the courtyard only. Observe the dress code and keep quiet. The entry fee is informal (20–50 som) — ask what you are paying for; sometimes they ask for money “for the children”. Don't confuse it with other mosques in Karakol — you want the Central Ibrahim-azhy mosque at 142a Abdrakhmanov.
kg-0081.food: Ashlan-fu — a Dungan cold noodle dish with starch jelly; in Karakol it is made at the Ak-Tilek bazaar and in cafes by the market (~90 som with flatbread, 2024); Dungan manti and lagman; local apricots and honey at the market.
kg-0081.reviews: Google Maps (“Dungan mosque”): 4.5/5, 1820 ratings as of 03.10.2026. 2GIS “Central Ibrahim Azhy Mosque”: 5/5, 311 ratings (07.10.2026). TripAdvisor “Dungan Mosque”: 3.9/5, 199 reviews, no. 6 of 40 in Karakol (07.10.2026). Pros: unique “Chinese” architecture, colours, quiet; cons: you're often not let inside, the grounds are small and cramped for photos, the visit is short, the entry fee is unclear.
kg-0081.p.sum: The mosque stands in the centre of Karakol (the corner of Abdrakhmanov and Bektenov streets), 10–15 minutes on foot from the square and the bazaar. The overnight GoBus from Bishkek (700 som) arrives at 05:40 right at the mosque. Entry to the courtyard is 20–50 som, open to tourists roughly 06:00–21:00 (Nomad's Land). On Friday 13:00–14:30 you aren't admitted inside. Allow 30–40 minutes for the visit. Combine it with the Holy Trinity Cathedral (1 km) and ashlan-fu in the “ashlan-fu row” at the bazaar. Stay in Karakol hostels from $7 in a dorm.

kg-0082.name: Chon-Kyzyl-Suu Gorge
kg-0082.near: Kyzyl-Suu (formerly Pokrovka), the district centre, ~30 km west of Karakol; from the village ~25 km up the gorge to the geophysical station.
kg-0082.elev: Valley floor in the lower part ~2,000 m; Jyluu-Suu hot springs 2,340 m; hut 2,500–2,550 m; geophysical station 2,600 m (Destination Jeti-Oguz, Nomad's Land); ridge up to 4,500 m, Kyzyl-Suu peak.
kg-0082.short: Chon-Kyzyl-Suu is a gorge south of Kyzyl-Suu with red cliffs in the lower part, the hot sulphur springs of Jyluu-Suu (43–45 °C), an old geophysical station-hut at 2,600 m and routes to lakes and glaciers.
kg-0082.desc: The Chon-Kyzyl-Suu gorge (“big red water”) begins at the district centre Kyzyl-Suu and over 25 km climbs from ~1,800 to 2,600 m. The river got its name from the muddy red colour of the water eroding red sandstones. 15–20 km from the village are the Jyluu-Suu hot sulphur springs (43–45 °C) in simple concrete baths, and another 4 km on is the old geophysical station of the Tian Shan Observatory, which works as a hut (a room with 4 beds, a Kyrgyz floor room, a Russian banya (sauna), camping, horses, guides) at the fork of the Karabatkak and Ashuu-Tor gorges. Higher up are Lake Savator (Salvator), the Ashuu-Tor waterfalls, the Shatyly cascade (100 m) and Sharkyratma (20 m), the Karabatkak glacier with its lake, and Kyzyl-Suu peak. The Archa-Tor, Savator and Teleti passes link the valley with Jeti-Oguz and the Karakol gorge; routes also lead on to Altyn-Arashan. Snow leopard, bear, ibex and marmots live here. The road is paved at the village, then dirt with fords, a 4x4 or a local driver is needed; the season is May — October.
kg-0082.guide: Drive into the gorge from Kyzyl-Suu without hurrying: the first kilometres are red cliffs, from which the river got its “red” name, then spruce and sea buckthorn. After 15–20 km by the river are the concrete Jyluu-Suu baths with 43–45 °C water: a Soviet bathhouse without gloss, but almost without people; sometimes there is no one even to take the fee. Another 4 km and you are at the geophysical station: here you can spend the night at 2,600 m, steam in a Russian banya and in the morning go to Lake Savator or the waterfall in Ashuu-Tor; arrange horses with the hosts. If you plan a trek to Jeti-Oguz via Archa-Tor — set out from here, it is 2–3 days. From below, drive only in a 4×4 or with a local driver: after rain the fords rise, and there is no phone coverage above the village.
kg-0082.see: The Jyluu-Suu hot springs (43–45 °C, sulphur); the geophysical station-hut at 2,600 m; Lake Savator; the waterfall in the Ashuu-Tor gorge, the Shatyly cascade (100 m) and Sharkyratma (20 m); the Karabatkak glacier with its lake; the red cliffs of the lower part; sea buckthorn and barberry at 2,000 m; birds wintering by the warm springs.
kg-0082.skip: You have no 4×4 or budget for a driver — it is 15–25 km uphill on foot from the village. You want well-appointed thermal baths — here are Soviet-style concrete tubs. You are choosing between this gorge and Jeti-Oguz with one day — Jeti-Oguz is more accessible and more spectacular for a short visit.
kg-0082.diff: The drive to the springs and station — moderate (dirt, fords, 4x4); walks near the station — easy; trips to Savator, the waterfalls and the glacier — moderate (one-day side trips with 300–700 m of gain); crossings of the Archa-Tor/Teleti passes — hard (3,500–3,800 m, 2–3 days).
kg-0082.when: May — October (saigatours: in winter the road is closed by snow); July — September for treks to the glacier and passes; the springs are pleasant in the cold months too, if the road is passable.
kg-0082.hours: An open area, around the clock (Google Maps: “Daily: 24 hours”). The springs have no fixed hours, the attendant is not always there; the hut at the station — by arrangement/booking (Nomad's Land, Destination Jeti-Oguz).
kg-0082.daytime: Leave Kyzyl-Suu in the morning (fords are lower, and you can return by daylight); soak in the springs in the evening after a trek; the red cliffs of the lower part look best in low sun.
kg-0082.how: From Karakol 30 km west to Kyzyl-Suu (marshrutka (minibus)/taxi), then south up the gorge: the asphalt quickly gives way to dirt, ~15–20 km to the Jyluu-Suu springs and ~25 km to the geophysical station (4x4 or a local driver). On foot/by bicycle along the road is an option for the prepared. Hiking entries: from Jeti-Oguz over the Archa-Tor pass, from the Karakol gorge over Teleti.
kg-0082.needcar: Yes: to Kyzyl-Suu — marshrutka/taxi; up the gorge — a 4×4 or a local driver; above the station — on foot or by horse.
kg-0082.self: Yes, with a 4×4 or on foot/by bicycle; no permits; an overnight at the hut by arrangement or in a tent. For the passes experience and a map are needed; no phone coverage.
kg-0082.roadtype: Paved in Kyzyl-Suu, then a dirt road along the river with bridges and fords (issykkul.biz), for a 4x4 or high clearance; above the station — trails.
kg-0082.traveltime: Karakol — Kyzyl-Suu 30 km, ~40 min; Kyzyl-Suu — springs 15–20 km, ~1 h; — station 25 km, 1.5–2 h (Nomad's Land: the whole way from Karakol 58 km, ~3 h 15 min with stops). Side trips from the station: to Savator and the waterfalls — 3–6 h; over Archa-Tor to Jeti-Oguz — 2–3 days.
kg-0082.stay: The hut at the geophysical station (2,500–2,600 m): a room with 4 beds, a Kyrgyz floor room, a Russian banya, camping, meals at a local family (Destination Jeti-Oguz, Nomad's Land; price not published). At the springs — a guesthouse with national cuisine (Nomad's Land). Guesthouses in Kyzyl-Suu “from $4–7 per person” (issykkul.biz, undated). The Ak-Tash yurt camp in the upper reaches (Wanderlog, not confirmed).
kg-0082.net: Kyzyl-Suu has coverage; higher up the gorge, at the springs and the station — no phone coverage (general reports; operators not checked separately).
kg-0082.entry: Free in the gorge. The Jyluu-Suu hot springs — a symbolic fee of “less than $5” (up to ~400 som), sometimes there is no one to accept payment (saigatours, 2024–2025). The exact 2026 tariff in som is not confirmed.
kg-0082.transfer: Carriers’ prices are not published; Nomad's Land and Destination Jeti-Oguz — on request. A guide from neighbouring routes: a 4×4 with a driver from Karakol for the day 5,000 som (Tosor/Jeti-Oguz/Barskoon, 2024).
kg-0082.bring: Swimwear and a towel for the springs, warm layers (nights at 2,600 m are cold), a rain jacket, boots for fords and trails, cash (hut, springs, horses), food for the day, an offline map/GPS, a torch, a first-aid kit; for trekking — a tent and sleeping bag.
kg-0082.warn: The road has fords — after rain and during snowmelt the river rises and a passenger car cannot pass. No phone coverage above the village. Sulphur springs of 43–45 °C — do not sit longer than 15–20 min, do not bathe after alcohol. In the upper reaches — wild animals (bear), herders’ dogs. In 2022 a SaryTours article described the location differently — follow the Destination Jeti-Oguz description via Kyzyl-Suu.
kg-0082.food: National dishes at the guesthouse by the springs and at the family at the station (beshbarmak, lagman, kumys in summer); sea buckthorn and barberry in the lower part (in season); in Kyzyl-Suu — a bazaar with local produce and cafes.
kg-0082.reviews: Google Maps (“Chon-Kyzyl-Suu gorge”, a point near Ayu-Tor/Jyluu-Suu): 4.9/5, 27 ratings as of 03.10.2026. TripAdvisor/2GIS: no separate listing for the gorge found. From 2024–2025 blogs: pros — wild hot springs with almost no people, a hut with a banya, a beautiful road; cons — a hard access road, primitive baths, no phone coverage.
kg-0082.p.sum: From Karakol — a marshrutka to Kyzyl-Suu (≈40 som, 30 km), then a local taxi up the gorge: the first 10 km ≈200 som, the next 10 km ≈400 som (Against the Compass), or your own 4×4. 15 km from the village are the hot concrete baths of Jyluu-Suu (43–45 °C, up to $5); from them ≈5 km on foot (1.5 h) to the geophysical (weather) station at 2,580 m: a hut for 18 with no electricity or running water, a banya, horses, guides. Stay overnight at the Ak-Tash yurt camp (12 places, three meals a day and a banya) or at the station. In the morning — a side trip to the Karabatkak glacier and lake (14 km, +700 m, 6 h). A horse crossing to Jeti-Oguz over the Ak-Sai pass (2,805 m) — 21 km in 6 h, on foot over Archa-Tor (3,900 m) — 3–4 days.

kg-0083.name: Lake Besh-Tash
kg-0083.near: Beshtash — ~6.3 km as the crow flies (OSM marker, catalog calculation; in reality a small settlement/ranger post in the gorge). Kozhuchak is the village at the entrance to the gorge; the town of Talas is 47 km to the north (too.kg).
kg-0083.elev: About 3000 m (too.kg, nomad.kg, map.kg); central-asia.guide — 2997 m. The start of the walking section in the TUK program is 2675 m.
kg-0083.short: A turquoise high-mountain lake (~3000 m, 28 m deep) at the end of the 30 km Besh-Tash gorge — the main goal of the nature park of the same name, 47 km south of Talas.
kg-0083.desc: Besh-Tash is the largest of the eight mountain lakes of the Besh-Tash nature park in the Talas Ala-Too (too.kg). The lake lies at an elevation of about 3000 m, is 28 m deep and covers about 0.5 km² (central-asia.guide; too.kg); the water is turquoise, and there is a small unnamed lake below the main one (too.kg). Trout, marinka (snowtrout) and osman (Tien Shan scaly osman) live in the lake and river (map.kg, 2024). The name “Besh-Tash” means “five stones”: in the gorge stand five stones tied to a legend about robbers (too.kg). The road runs along the Besh-Tash River almost up to the moraine below the lake; per too.kg it is a 15-minute walk from the end of the road to the water, but per nomad.kg an ordinary car only reaches the park checkpoint, and the last 20–25 km are on foot or by 4×4 / SUV.
kg-0083.guide: Besh-Tash is a rare case where you can see a 3,000-metre lake without a multi-day trek: by 4×4 / SUV through the gorge almost to the moraine, and then 15 minutes on foot to the turquoise water. If you are in an ordinary car, leave it at the park checkpoint and allow a day for the 20–25 km through the gorge — or camp in a tent by the lake, there are plenty of campsites. Along the way look out for those very “five stones” that gave the gorge its name. There is no mobile signal; drink water from the lake and river only after boiling. The best time is July — August, when it is warm and yurts stand in the gorge.
kg-0083.see: Turquoise Lake Besh-Tash and the small lake below; the moraine below the lake; the Besh-Tash gorge with juniper, spruce and Semenov fir; the “five stones” that gave the gorge its name; flowering meadows in May — June (too.kg; nomad.kg).
kg-0083.skip: You have an ordinary passenger car and no spare day for a 20–25 km walk from the checkpoint. You are not ready for a night at 3000 m without a signal or infrastructure. You want a “lake with services” — there is no cafe or lodging here.
kg-0083.diff: Easy with a 4×4 / SUV (15 min on foot from the moraine — too.kg); moderate on foot from the checkpoint (20–25 km one way through the gorge — nomad.kg) or in the TUK program (start 2675 m, ~325 m of climbing to 3000 m). Altitude 3000 m.
kg-0083.when: July — August: passes are open, it is warm, yurt camps operate (nomad.kg); May — June — tulips and blooms (but ice and snow may lie by the lake); September — golden autumn. too.kg advises April — May to catch the ice melt — at 3000 m the approach may be blocked by snow at that time (not confirmed). In winter access is limited.
kg-0083.hours: Through the checkpoint of the Besh-Tash nature park with payment of a fee; the checkpoint's opening hours are not published.
kg-0083.daytime: Morning — smooth water and a rich turquoise colour before clouds and wind (editorial).
kg-0083.how: From Talas south ~13 km to the entrance of the Besh-Tash gorge (central-asia.guide), then along a dirt road beside the river: an ordinary car goes as far as the park checkpoint, the remaining 20–25 km are on foot or by 4×4 / SUV (nomad.kg); too.kg writes that a good dirt road reaches almost to the lake, with a 15-minute walk from the moraine. About 47 km in total from Talas. From Bishkek to Talas — 5.5–8 h (marshrutka (minibus)/taxi via Otmok or GoBus via Kazakhstan).
kg-0083.needcar: Yes: a taxi/your own car from Talas; to get close to the lake — a 4×4 / SUV (otherwise on foot from the checkpoint).
kg-0083.self: Yes: no border permit is needed, just pay the park fee at the checkpoint. Without a 4×4 / SUV — a long walk in; there is no signal — tell someone your route.
kg-0083.roadtype: A dirt road through the gorge along the Besh-Tash River; to the checkpoint — passable for passenger cars, beyond that a 4×4 / SUV (nomad.kg); too.kg describes the road as a good dirt road almost to the lake. From the moraine — a 15 min trail.
kg-0083.traveltime: Talas — park checkpoint ~30–40 min (estimate); checkpoint — lake: 20–25 km, ~1.5–2 h by 4×4 / SUV or 6–8 h on foot one way (estimate based on nomad.kg); from the moraine — 15 min on foot (too.kg). From Bishkek to the park — about 4–5 h by car (map.kg says “about 4 hours”).
kg-0083.stay: By the lake — tents only, with plenty of campsites (too.kg); the park has equipped camping zones at various elevations, campfires are allowed (map.kg, 2024); in summer yurt camps operate in the gorge (nomad.kg; names and prices not found). Guesthouses are in Talas ($10–30) and through CBT Talas.
kg-0083.net: There is no mobile signal at the lake (too.kg; visitsilkroad.org).
kg-0083.entry: Besh-Tash nature park fee: 250 som per person and 400 som per vehicle (nomad.kg; publication year not given). The official Forest Service price list was not found.
kg-0083.transfer: Not confirmed: prices for a 4×4 / SUV or taxi Talas — lake are not published. To Talas: GoBus 500 som (2025), marshrutka (minibus) ~350 som, shared taxi from ~650 som.
kg-0083.bring: A tent and a warm sleeping bag (a night at 3000 m), a down jacket, a rain jacket, a stove and means of boiling/purifying water (drink water from the lake and river only after boiling — visitsilkroad.org), food for the whole trip, cash for the park fee (250 + 400 som), sun protection.
kg-0083.warn: No mobile signal. At 3000 m altitude sickness is possible, and nights are cold even in summer. Boil water. Brown bears live in the park (central-asia.guide) — store food properly. Do not drink or wash with soap in the lake. In a passenger car you can only get as far as the checkpoint; in bad weather the dirt road gets washed out.
kg-0083.food: At the gorge's yurt camps in summer — kumis and shepherds' home food (not confirmed for specific places); in Talas — dishes with Talas beans.
kg-0083.reviews: Google Maps: 5.0 from 10 ratings (catalog check, 10.2026). No reviews with a meaningful sample were found on TripAdvisor or 2GIS; descriptions note the turquoise colour of the water and easy access by 4×4 / SUV.
kg-0083.p.sum: Lake Besh-Tash (~3000 m) is a 1–2 day objective from Talas: 13 km of paved road to the gorge entrance at Kozhuchak, payment at the park's automatic checkpoint (since 28.07.2026, by card/QR), then a dirt road — a passenger car as far as the checkpoint, a 4×4 / SUV higher up to the camp meadows (~2675 m); from there 6 km on foot (12 km round trip, +325 m). The most convenient is a 4×4 / SUV from Talas or a Trekking Union group trip (5500 som). Camp in a tent in the park or stay in Talas.

kg-0084.name: Kalmak-Ashuu Pass
kg-0084.near: Sary-Bulak — the turn to Kalmak-Ashuu is about 3 km from the village on the Bishkek — Torugart highway (too.kg). The nearest base with services is Kochkor. The earlier “Ken-Suu ~21.6 km” is a straight-line distance from an offset point and is no guide for a traveler.
kg-0084.elev: 3446–3447 m (Trip to Kyrgyzstan, NomadCar, central-asia.live — 3447 m; Nomad's Land, open.kg, OunTravela — 3446 m).
kg-0084.short: Kalmak-Ashuu (3446 m) is a gravel pass over the Song-Kol-Too range, the shortest and most popular road route from Kochkor and Sary-Bulak to the northeast shore of Song-Kol.
kg-0084.desc: The pass links the Bishkek — Naryn highway (the turn near Sary-Bulak) with the Song-Kol basin. The eastern ascent is a steep, stony road through a gorge among scree slopes; the western descent to the lake is gentle, across alpine meadows with edelweiss and herds of yaks. There is constant wind at the top, so there are no yurts on the saddle itself. The road opens in late May (cleared by a snowplow) and closes with the first snow in late October. According to legend, the name is linked to raids by the Kalmyks (Dzungars) on the Kyrgyz at the Song-Kol pastures (Nomad's Land). OunTravela (2026) calls Kalmak-Ashuu the easiest of the passes to Song-Kol — a well-kept gravel road; it is popular with cyclists.
kg-0084.guide: Stop on the Kalmak-Ashuu saddle: from here the Song-Kol basin opens up for the first time — the moment many people take this route for. Up the eastern side the road climbs in steep, stony loops among scree, so don't rush your driver, and at the top keep your jacket handy — the wind here is such that herders don't pitch yurts. Look for edelweiss on the meadows of the western slope and for herds of yaks. A legend says the pass was named by the Kalmyks who once raided the Song-Kol camps. If you're planning a loop route, it's convenient to leave by going down via Moldo-Ashuu to the south or via 33 Parrots to the southeast.
kg-0084.see: The first view of the Song-Kol basin from the 3446 m saddle; the gorge with scree and serpentine on the eastern ascent; alpine meadows with edelweiss on the western slope; herds of yaks; on the way, the Song-Kol-Too and Bay-Dulu ranges (almost 4000 m).
kg-0084.skip: You're going to Song-Kol from the south (from Chayek or Naryn) — Moldo-Ashuu, Kara-Keche or 33 Parrots suit you better. You have an ordinary sedan and no experience with gravel serpentines. You're traveling in November to May: the road is closed by snow.
kg-0084.diff: Moderate for a car: gravel, a steep stony eastern ascent, a gentle western descent; OunTravela (2026) — “the easiest of the passes to Song-Kol”. You need a crossover/4×4 / SUV with good ground clearance (NomadCar). For cyclists, a hard but popular climb.
kg-0084.when: July to September. The road opens in late May after snow clearing and closes in late October (Nomad's Land); Trip to Kyrgyzstan and NomadCar say “June to October”. The herders leave Song-Kol before the pass closes (September).
kg-0084.hours: An open dirt road with no barriers; seasonal — roughly from late May/June to late October, impassable in winter because of snow.
kg-0084.daytime: Morning and the first half of the day: less wind and cloud, soft light on the Song-Kol basin; after rain or at dusk the gravel loops are dangerous (editorial).
kg-0084.how: From Bishkek along the highway toward Naryn via Balykchy and Kochkor to Sary-Bulak; about 3 km from the village is the turn to Kalmak-Ashuu (too.kg), then a gravel climb over the pass and a descent to the northeast shore of Song-Kol. Bishkek — Kochkor about 230 km (~4 h), Kochkor — Song-Kol about 80 km (~2.5 h) according to topologica (2026).
kg-0084.needcar: Yes — a 4×4 / SUV/crossover or an organized transfer; there is no public transport over the pass. An alternative is a bicycle.
kg-0084.self: Yes, in your own/rented car with ground clearance in season; no permit needed. Without a car — only by transfer.
kg-0084.roadtype: Gravel/dirt: the eastern ascent is a steep stony road through a gorge among scree, the western descent is gentle across meadows (Nomad's Land). OunTravela (09.2026) — “a well-kept gravel road”. topologica (2026) warns of deep ruts and the need for high ground clearance.
kg-0084.traveltime: Kochkor — Song-Kol via Kalmak-Ashuu ~80 km / ~2.5 h; Bishkek — Kochkor ~230 km / ~4 h (topologica, 2026). In all, Bishkek — the north shore of Song-Kol ~6.5–7 h with stops (calculated).
kg-0084.stay: There is no accommodation on the pass (because of the wind there are no yurts either — Nomad's Land). Stay overnight in the yurt camps on the north shore of Song-Kol: roughly $15–25/person for budget, $35–50 mid-range, $60–80 full board (topologica, 2026 — estimate, check with CBT Kochkor/Shepherd's Life) — or in Kochkor guesthouses.
kg-0084.net: At Song-Kol the signal is “partial, in places” (too.kg); topologica (2026) reports no mobile signal at most camps. On the pass, operator coverage is not confirmed — rely on offline maps.
kg-0084.entry: Free: no fee for crossing the pass was found. (Separate eco fees at Song-Kol are not confirmed within this entry.)
kg-0084.transfer: Pegas Adventure: Kochkor — Song-Kol via Kalmak-Ashuu — $200 (1 person), $120/person (2), $90/person (3), $80/person (4–12); topologica (2026): $60–80 per car / $15–20 per person with 4 passengers. Marshrutka (minibus) Bishkek — Kochkor — 350 som (CBT Naryn, 05.2026).
kg-0084.bring: A windbreaker and a warm layer (3446 m, strong wind), sunglasses and sunscreen, water and a snack, offline maps; for the driver — a spare tire and a full tank (the last fuel is in Kochkor/Sary-Bulak).
kg-0084.warn: The pass is impassable from late October to late May because of snow. Elevation 3446 m: a same-day climb from Bishkek can cause a headache. In rain the gravel and the loops of the eastern slope are slippery; don't take a sedan. Constant strong wind on the saddle.
kg-0084.food: There is no food on the pass. In the Song-Kol yurt camps — kumys, fresh kaymak, boorsok, beshbarmak (topologica: premium camps include 3 meals, tea and kumys in the price). Before the climb — cafes in Sary-Bulak.
kg-0084.reviews: Google Maps: 5/5, 2 ratings (as of 03.10.2026, from the catalog check). No separate TripAdvisor listing was found. Reviews and blogs (OunTravela, Nomad's Land) mention a spectacular view of Song-Kol and easy gravel; cons — wind, the steep stony ascent, winter closure.
kg-0084.p.sum: Kalmak-Ashuu (3446 m) is the shortest road approach from Kochkor to the northeast shore of Song-Kol: along the highway toward Naryn to Sary-Bulak, a turn after ~3 km, then gravel over the pass — ≈80 km/2.5 h from Kochkor. Open from late May to late October; in dry weather a crossover/SUV can manage it, a sedan is not advised (stony eastern ascent, ruts). Without a car — a 4×4 from Kochkor (≈5200 som per car per 2026 data) or a Pegas Adventure transfer. Fill up in Kochkor; on the pass there are no yurts or services.

kg-0086.name: Koshoy-Korgon Fortress
kg-0086.full: Koshoy-Korgon fortress site and the Koshoy-Korgon archaeological and ethnographic museum
kg-0086.near: Kara-Suu village — the fortress is about 2 km southeast (eurasia.travel); access via village streets (Lonely Planet: 800 m along the eastern Kyocher street, then left on Abit street). At-Bashy village — about 12–15 km (ilovekg, Journal of Nomads, eurasia.travel); the town of Naryn — about an hour's drive. Note: ilovekg wrongly says “12 km west of Naryn”.
kg-0086.elev: About 2100 m (Nomad's Land — 2107 m). eurasia.travel mentions a “plateau at 2500 m” — that describes the surroundings, not the site itself.
kg-0086.short: Koshoy-Korgon is a medieval fortress town (7th/8th–12th centuries, capital of medieval At-Bashy) with mud-brick walls 245–250 m on each side near the village of Kara-Suu, and a small archaeological and ethnographic museum at the entrance; it is on the UNESCO Tentative List.
kg-0086.desc: The rectangular fortress, 245–250 m across, is surrounded by walls of mud brick and long brick: 7–9 m thick at the base, with a surviving height of 4–8 m (Nomad's Land; up to 10 m according to eurasia.travel). Dozens of towers can be traced along the walls (Nomad's Land counts 60, eurasia.travel about 50), along with a moat 11–14 m wide. The site has been inhabited since at least the 8th century, flourished in the 9th–12th centuries, and its main citadel dates to the Karakhanid era (12th century); it is seen as the medieval town of At-Bash on the Silk Road between Kashgar and Naryn. By the western wall are the remains of a minaret, and in the south are excavations linked to the ruler's residence. According to legend, the fortress was built by Koshoy, a companion and adviser of Manas. The site is on the UNESCO Tentative List (“Nomadic Monuments of the Inner Tian Shan”). At the entrance is a museum built in 2007 with the support of the Dordoi association (gallery since 2010): finds from Koshoy-Korgon and other sites of Naryn region, ethnography and an art collection.
kg-0086.guide: Walk the path along the crest of the old ramparts — it's the best way to grasp the scale: a square of almost 250 by 250 meters with towers around the perimeter. On the west side look for the remains of the minaret, and in the south for the excavations where, according to tradition, the ruler's house stood. Locals link the fortress with Koshoy, Manas's uncle and adviser, although archaeologists date it to the 8th–12th centuries. The museum at the entrance opens irregularly — call or ask the caretaker in Kara-Suu in advance. The best light is at dawn or in the evening: there's no shade in the daytime, so bring water and a hat.
kg-0086.see: Mud-brick walls and towers around the perimeter (245–250 m); the path along the crest of the ramparts; the remains of the minaret by the western wall; excavations by the southern wall; the moat; the Koshoy-Korgon museum at the entrance (artifacts of Naryn region, weapons, utensils, clothing, an art gallery).
kg-0086.skip: You expect a restored fortress like Tash-Rabat — here there are weathered earthen ramparts, interesting more for their scale and history. The museum matters to you and you couldn't arrange for it to be opened. You don't like short stops — it takes only 60–90 minutes in all.
kg-0086.diff: Easy: you can drive almost to the entrance, and the walk over level ground and the ramparts takes 60–90 minutes (ilovekg).
kg-0086.when: May to October; in summer it's hot and shadeless, and after rain the dirt access road turns to mud (ilovekg). In winter the site is accessible, but it is cold and snowy.
kg-0086.hours: The fortress grounds are open, with no fenced entrance. Museum: no regular schedule, “opens rarely” — call or look for the caretaker in advance (ilovekg, Lonely Planet, tury.ru).
kg-0086.daytime: Dawn or evening — soft light on the ramparts and less heat; there's no shade in the daytime (ilovekg).
kg-0086.how: From Naryn along the Naryn — Torugart highway to km 409, at the village of Kara-Suu turn off (about 3 km from the highway — Lonely Planet), then along Kyocher and Abit streets to the fortress. From Naryn it's about an hour's drive (Journal of Nomads). It's easy to combine with a trip to Tash-Rabat — it's the same road.
kg-0086.needcar: Yes: car/taxi from Naryn or At-Bashy; public transport doesn't run for the last kilometers (ilovekg).
kg-0086.self: Yes: no permit needed, the site is open; for the museum, arrange it in advance.
kg-0086.roadtype: The paved Naryn — Torugart highway, then about 3 km through the village and a dirt/gravel road to the fortress (muddy after rain — ilovekg).
kg-0086.traveltime: Naryn — Koshoy-Korgon about 1 h (Journal of Nomads); from At-Bashy 15–20 min (calculated, 12–15 km); Bishkek — Naryn ~5–6 h.
kg-0086.stay: There is no accommodation at the fortress. Options are guesthouses in At-Bashy and Naryn (CBT Naryn), and yurt camps near Tash-Rabat (1500–2000 som/person with breakfast and dinner — snoezelsontheroad, 2025–2026).
kg-0086.net: Not confirmed by operator coverage maps; the village of Kara-Suu and the Torugart highway are nearby, so there is probably a mobile signal (not verified).
kg-0086.entry: The fortress grounds are free (no fenced ticket office). The museum ticket price is not given in the sources (Lonely Planet: “no admission price listed”) — ask the caretaker.
kg-0086.transfer: Not confirmed: taxi prices Naryn — Koshoy-Korgon were not found in the sources. Marshrutka (minibus) Bishkek — Naryn — 600 som (CBT Naryn, 05.2026).
kg-0086.bring: Water, a hat and sunscreen (no shade — ilovekg); comfortable shoes for walking on the ramparts; cash for the museum; the caretaker's number/an arrangement for your visit.
kg-0086.warn: The museum opens irregularly — without calling ahead you may see only the ramparts. Don't climb on crumbling sections of the walls and don't dig or take pottery — this is an archaeological monument (UNESCO Tentative List). The access road turns to mud after rain.
kg-0086.food: No cafe was found at the fortress; eat in At-Bashy or Naryn. Traditional dishes in the Naryn region are beshbarmak, shorpo and kumys (editorial).
kg-0086.reviews: Google Maps: 4.5/5, 106 ratings (as of 03.10.2026, catalog check). Lonely Planet lists the site among the attractions of Naryn region. Pros: the scale of the ramparts, the path along the walls, the link to the Manas epic; cons: the closed museum, few surviving structures, no shade.
kg-0086.p.sum: Koshoy-Korgon is a short stop on the way Naryn → Tash-Rabat/Kel-Suu: about 1 h from Naryn, 15–20 min from At-Bashy. No permit needed. On the Naryn — Torugart highway at the village of Kara-Suu, turn left after the mosque and memorial and drive to the end of the street (≈2–3 km) — the ramparts are in a field on the right, with a private museum next to them (the caretaker speaks Russian/Kyrgyz, the museum costs extra). 30–60 min is enough to look around; stay overnight in At-Bashy or in the yurts at Tash-Rabat.
